sub_modules.title: Nervous & Endocrine Systems: Electrophysiology, Synaptic Transmission & Signal Transduction
sub_modules.overview: Rapid electrical signaling across neuronal membranes (governed by voltage-gated ion channels and the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation) integrates with slower, amplified hormonal cascades (GPCRs, RTKs, and nuclear receptors) through the hypothalamic-pituitary neuroendocrine axis.

core_concepts.heading: Resting Potential, Action Potential Biophysics & Synaptic Transmission
core_concepts.theory: A resting mammalian neuron maintains an electrical potential of Vm ≈ -70 mV (inside negative) generated by the electrogenic Na+/K+-ATPase (3 Na+ out : 2 K+ in) and high resting membrane permeability to K+ via two-pore domain K+ (K2P) leak channels, keeping Vm close to the K+ Nernst equilibrium potential (EK ≈ -90 mV vs. ENa ≈ +60 mV).
key_principles: Hodgkin-Huxley Action Potential Phases: (1) Threshold (-55 mV): Graded excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) summate at the axon hillock; (2) Depolarization Upstroke: Voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav1.x) snap open (activation m-gate), increasing P_Na 500-fold and driving Vm toward ENa (+30 to +40 mV overshoot); (3) Repolarization: Rapid time-dependent closure of the Nav inactivation ball-and-chain h-gate plus delayed opening of voltage-gated K+ channels (Kv, n-gate) drives K+ efflux; (4) Hyperpolarization (Undershoot): Slow Kv closure briefly pulls Vm toward EK (-80 mV).

Absolute vs. Relative Refractory Periods & Saltatory Conduction: During the Absolute Refractory Period, Nav inactivation h-gates are locked shut—no stimulus of any magnitude can trigger a second spike, enforcing unidirectional propagation. Myelin sheaths (Schwann cells in PNS; Oligodendrocytes in CNS) increase transmembrane resistance (Rm) and decrease capacitance (Cm), increasing the length constant (λ = √(Rm/Ri)) so action potentials leap between Nodes of Ranvier (Saltatory Conduction up to 120 m/s).

Chemical Synaptic Transmission: Arrival of the action potential at the presynaptic bouton opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Cav2.1/2.2). Ca2+ influx binds Synaptotagmin, catalyzing SNARE complex (Synaptobrevin, Syntaxin-1, SNAP-25) zippering and vesicle exocytosis of neurotransmitters: Glutamate (AMPA/NMDA excitatory cation channels) vs. GABA/Glycine (GABAA/GlyR inhibitory Cl- channels).

core_concepts.heading: Endocrine Axes, GPCR Second Messengers & Receptor Tyrosine Kinases
core_concepts.theory: Hormones are classified into lipid-soluble steroids/thyroid hormones (which diffuse across plasma membranes to bind intracellular nuclear receptors acting as zinc-finger transcription factors) and water-soluble peptides/catecholamines (which bind cell-surface GPCRs or RTKs).
key_principles: Heterotrimeric G-Protein Coupled Receptors (7-TM GPCRs): Ligand binding induces a conformational shift in the 7-transmembrane helix bundle, acting as a Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factor (GEF) that swaps GDP for GTP on the Gα subunit (dissociating Gα-GTP from Gβγ): (1) Gαs (Glucagon, Epinephrine β-receptors, ACTH, TSH): activates Adenylate Cyclase -> converts ATP to cAMP -> activates Protein Kinase A (PKA); Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαs Arg201, locking it ON; (2) Gαi (Somatostatin, α2-adrenergic): inhibits Adenylate Cyclase; Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαi, locking it OFF; (3) Gαq (Angiotensin II, Vasopressin V1, α1-adrenergic): activates Phospholipase Cβ (PLCβ) -> cleaves PIP2 into IP3 (opens ER IP3R Ca2+ channels) and DAG (activates Protein Kinase C, PKC).

Receptor Tyrosine Kinases (RTKs — Insulin & Growth Factors): Insulin binds the preformed α2β2 Insulin Receptor tetramer, triggering trans-autophosphorylation of cytosolic tyrosine residues, which recruits IRS-1 -> PI3K (PIP2 -> PIP3) -> PDK1 -> Akt (PKB) to translocate GLUT4 vesicles to the muscle/adipocyte plasma membrane and activate glycogen synthase.

sub_modules.title: Cardiovascular & Respiratory Physiology: Hemodynamics, Frank-Starling & Hemoglobin Cooperativity
sub_modules.overview: The cardiovascular and pulmonary systems operate in series to convective-diffusively transport O2 from alveolar air (PO2 = 100–104 mmHg) to respiring tissues (PO2 = 20–40 mmHg) while exporting CO2 and buffering blood pH at 7.40.

core_concepts.heading: Cardiac Automaticity, The Cardiac Cycle & Frank-Starling Hemodynamics
core_concepts.theory: Rhythmic cardiac contraction originates autonomously in the Sinoatrial (SA) Node pacemaker (60–100 bpm), where hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 'funny' Na+ channels (HCN / If) and T-type/L-type Ca2+ channels drive spontaneous diastolic depolarization (Phase 4) without a true resting potential.
key_principles: Conduction Delay & Ventricular Action Potential (Phase 2 Plateau): Impulse spreads from SA Node -> Internodal pathways -> Atrioventricular (AV) Node (~100 ms delay allowing atrial contraction/ventricular filling) -> Bundle of His -> Purkinje fibers. Ventricular cardiomyocytes exhibit a prolonged 250–300 ms Action Potential due to Phase 2 L-type Ca2+ influx (Cav1.2) balancing K+ efflux (preventing tetanic summation). Ca2+ influx triggers Ryanodine Receptor (RyR2) Ca2+-Induced Ca2+ Release (CICR) from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Cardiac Output (CO), Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) & Poiseuille's Law: Cardiac Output is the product of Heart Rate and Stroke Volume (CO = HR × SV, where SV = EDV - ESV ≈ 120 mL - 50 mL = 70 mL). By Ohm's hydrodynamic analog, MAP - CVP = CO × TPR (Total Peripheral Resistance). Because resistance scales inversely with the fourth power of arteriolar radius (R = 8ηL / πr^4), a 19% constriction of arteriolar radius doubles vascular resistance.

The Frank-Starling Law of the Heart: Increased venous return increases End-Diastolic Volume (EDV, preload), stretching ventricular sarcomeres toward their optimal actomyosin overlap length (~2.2 μm) and increasing troponin C Ca2+ sensitivity, which intrinsically increases Stroke Volume to match venous input with arterial output.

core_concepts.heading: Allosteric Hemoglobin Cooperativity, The Bohr Effect & Acid-Base Transport
core_concepts.theory: Adult Hemoglobin (HbA, α2β2 tetramer) binds up to 4 O2 molecules via ferrous (Fe2+) protoporphyrin IX heme groups, exhibiting a sigmoidal O2 dissociation curve (P50 ≈ 26.8 mmHg, Hill coefficient nH ≈ 2.8–3.0) in contrast to monomeric Myoglobin's hyperbolic curve (P50 ≈ 2.8 mmHg, nH = 1.0).
key_principles: T-to-R Allosteric Transition (Perutz Mechanism): Deoxyhemoglobin exists in the low-affinity Tense (T) state stabilized by inter-subunit salt bridges (involving β-His146). Binding of O2 to the first heme pulls the Fe2+ ion ~0.04 nm into the porphyrin plane, dragging the proximal histidine (His F8) and α-helix F to rupture T-state salt bridges and shift the tetramer into the 150-fold higher-affinity Relaxed (R) state.

Right-Shift Allosteric Effectors ('CADET, face Right!'): Elevated CO2, Acid/H+ (decreased pH — the Bohr Effect), 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG, which binds the positively charged central cavity of β-chains in T-state HbA; fetal HbF [α2γ2] has Ser143 instead of His143, binding 2,3-BPG weakly so HbF has higher O2 affinity, P50 ≈ 19 mmHg), Exercise, and Temperature all stabilize the T-state, increasing P50 (shifting the curve right) to unload more O2 into metabolically active tissues.

CO2 Transport & The Haldane Effect: ~70% of tissue CO2 is converted inside erythrocytes by Carbonic Anhydrase (Zn2+ metalloenzyme) into H2CO3 -> H+ + HCO3-. While H+ is buffered by deoxy-Hb (His146), HCO3- is exported into plasma in exchange for Cl- via the AE1 (Band 3) anion exchanger (the Chloride Shift / Hamburger Phenomenon).

sub_modules.title: Renal, Digestive & Metabolic Integration: Nephron Clearance, Countercurrent Multiplication & Enzyme Kinetics
sub_modules.overview: Homeostasis of extracellular fluid volume, osmolarity, and metabolic fuel supply depends on glomerular filtration and countercurrent multiplication in the kidney alongside allosterically and hormonally regulated enzymatic pathways in the liver.

core_concepts.heading: Nephron Ultrafiltration, Starling Forces & Countercurrent Multiplication
core_concepts.theory: Each human kidney contains ~1 million nephrons. Blood enters the Glomerulus via the Afferent Arteriole and exits via the Efferent Arteriole; Starling hydrostatic and oncotic pressures drive ~20% of renal plasma flow across the fenestrated endothelium, negatively charged glomerular basement membrane (heparan sulfate), and podocyte slit diaphragms into Bowman's space (GFR ≈ 125 mL/min or 180 L/day).
key_principles: Tubular Reabsorption & Secretion Segments: (1) Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT): Reabsorbs 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids (via Na+ symporters SGLT2/SGLT1; renal threshold for glucose ~180–200 mg/dL) and ~67% of Na+, H2O, and HCO3- iso-osmotically (300 mOsm/L); (2) Loop of Henle (Countercurrent Multiplier): The Thin Descending Limb is permeable to H2O (via Aquaporin-1) but impermeable to NaCl; the Thick Ascending Limb (TAL) is impermeable to H2O ('diluting segment') and actively pumps solutes into the interstitium via the NKCC2 (Na+-K+-2Cl-) cotransporter (inhibited by Loop diuretics like Furosemide), generating a corticomedullary osmotic gradient from 300 mOsm/L to 1,200 mOsm/L; (3) Collecting Duct: Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH / Vasopressin via V2 GPCR -> cAMP -> PKA) inserts Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels into the apical membrane, allowing urine concentration up to 1,200 mOsm/L.

Renal Clearance Diagnostics (Inulin vs. PAH): Inulin (and endogenous Creatinine approximately) is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals the Glomerular Filtration Rate (C_inulin = GFR). Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is both filtered and 100% secreted by peritubular capillaries, so its clearance measures Effective Renal Plasma Flow (C_PAH = ERPF).

core_concepts.heading: Michaelis-Menten Enzyme Kinetics, Inhibition Modes & Metabolic Integration
core_concepts.theory: Enzymes accelerate biochemical reactions by 10^6- to 10^17-fold by stabilizing the high-energy Transition State (lowering activation free energy ΔG‡) without altering the overall equilibrium constant (K'_eq) or reaction ΔG.
key_principles: Briggs-Haldane Steady-State Derivation (Km & kcat): For E + S <-> ES -> E + P (with rate constants k1, k-1, and k2 = kcat), under the steady-state assumption d[ES]/dt = 0, the Michaelis constant is Km = (k-1 + kcat) / k1—representing the substrate concentration [S] at which initial velocity V0 = 1/2 Vmax (where Vmax = kcat [E]_total). The second-order specificity constant kcat / Km measures catalytic efficiency, reaching the diffusion-controlled physical limit of 10^8–10^9 M^-1·s^-1 in 'catalytically perfect' enzymes (e.g., Carbonic Anhydrase, Triosephosphate Isomerase, Acetylcholinesterase).

Reversible Enzyme Inhibition Mechanics: (1) Competitive Inhibition: Inhibitor (I) binds free Enzyme (E) at the active site (competing with S); increases apparent Km by factor α = 1 + [I]/Ki while Vmax remains unchanged (overcome by high [S]); (2) Pure Non-Competitive Inhibition: I binds equally to E and ES at an allosteric site (Ki = K'i); decreases apparent Vmax by factor α while Km remains unchanged; (3) Uncompetitive Inhibition: I binds exclusively to the ES complex; decreases BOTH apparent Vmax and apparent Km by the same factor α' = 1 + [I]/K'i (yielding parallel lines on a Lineweaver-Burk plot).

interactive_pins.label: Upstroke & Nav Inactivation (TTX Target)
interactive_pins.detail: Tetrodotoxin (TTX, pufferfish) and Saxitoxin plug the outer pore of voltage-gated Na+ channels (Kd ~ 1 nM), abolishing the action potential upstroke. Lidocaine blocks Nav from the intracellular side.

interactive_pins.label: Delayed K+ Efflux & Undershoot (TEA Target)
interactive_pins.detail: Tetraethylammonium (TEA) and 4-aminopyridine block voltage-gated K+ channels, prolonging repolarization and abolishing the hyperpolarizing undershoot.

interactive_pins.detail: Protonation of β-His146 in acidic tissues (pH 7.2) and binding of negatively charged 2,3-BPG stabilize the T-state, shifting P50 from 27 mmHg to ~35–40 mmHg to unload O2.

interactive_pins.label: Y-Axis Intersection (1/Vmax)
interactive_pins.detail: Competitive inhibitors intersect the uninhibited line directly on the Y-axis because infinite [S] (1/[S] -> 0) outcompetes the inhibitor completely.

solved_problems.title: Renal Physiology: Calculating GFR from Inulin Clearance & Net Glucose/PAH Tubular Handling
solved_problems.statement:
During a renal function clearance study, a patient receives an intravenous infusion of Inulin and Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH). Timed urine collection over 60 minutes yields a total urine volume of 120 mL. Laboratory analysis of plasma (P) and urine (U) reveals:
• Inulin: P_inulin = 1.00 mg/mL, U_inulin = 62.5 mg/mL
• PAH: P_PAH = 0.020 mg/mL, U_PAH = 6.00 mg/mL
• Glucose: P_Glc = 1.00 mg/mL (100 mg/dL), U_Glc = 0.00 mg/mL
Calculate: (a) the urine flow rate (V̇ in mL/min) and Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR), (b) the Effective Renal Plasma Flow (ERPF) and Filtration Fraction (FF = GFR / ERPF), and (c) the filtered load and net tubular reabsorption rate of glucose (in mg/min).

derivation_steps.explanation: Compute the urine flow rate V̇ (120 mL / 60 min) and apply the clearance equation C_inulin = (U_inulin · V̇) / P_inulin to find GFR:
derivation_steps.equation_latex: \dot{V} = \frac{120\text{ mL}}{60\text{ min}} = 2.00\text{ mL/min}, \qquad \text{GFR} = C_{\text{inulin}} = \frac{(62.5\text{ mg/mL})(2.00\text{ mL/min})}{1.00\text{ mg/mL}} = 125.0\text{ mL/min}

derivation_steps.explanation: Compute PAH clearance (which equals Effective Renal Plasma Flow, ERPF) and the Filtration Fraction (FF):
Calculate the Filtered Load of glucose (GFR × P_Glc) and subtract urinary excretion (U_Glc × V̇ = 0):
derivation_steps.equation_latex: \text{Filtered Load}_{\text{Glc}} = (125.0\text{ mL/min})(1.00\text{ mg/mL}) = 125.0\text{ mg/min} \implies \text{Reabsorption Rate} = 125.0 - 0 = 125.0\text{ mg/min (100\% reabsorbed in PCT)}

solved_problems.final_answer: (a) V̇ = 2.00 mL/min, GFR = 125.0 mL/min; (b) ERPF = 600.0 mL/min, Filtration Fraction = 20.8%; (c) Glucose filtered load = reabsorption rate = 125.0 mg/min (Glucose clearance = 0 mL/min).

solved_problems.title: Hemoglobin Cooperativity (Hill Equation) & Arterial-Venous O2 Delivery Capacity
solved_problems.statement: Normal human adult blood contains 15.0 g of Hemoglobin (HbA) per 100 mL (1 dL) of blood, and each gram of fully saturated HbA binds 1.34 mL of O2. Assume HbA has a P50 of 26.8 mmHg and a Hill cooperativity coefficient of n_H = 2.80. Given an arterial alveolar oxygen tension of P_aO2 = 100.0 mmHg and a resting venous tissue oxygen tension of P_vO2 = 40.0 mmHg: (a) Calculate the percentage O2 saturation (Y_O2) of HbA in arterial blood (100 mmHg) and in resting venous blood (40 mmHg) using the Hill equation. (b) Calculate the volume of O2 (in mL O2 per dL of blood) unloaded to the tissues during each circulatory pass.

derivation_steps.explanation: Evaluate the Hill equation Y = (PO2)^2.8 / [(26.8)^2.8 + (PO2)^2.8] at arterial P_aO2 = 100 mmHg (where 26.8^2.8 = 9,927 and 100^2.8 = 398,107):
Evaluate the Hill equation at resting venous P_vO2 = 40.0 mmHg (where 40.0^2.8 = 30,492):
Calculate the maximum O2-carrying capacity of 15.0 g Hb/dL (100% saturation) and multiply by the arterial-venous saturation difference (ΔY = 0.9757 - 0.7544 = 0.2213):
derivation_steps.equation_latex: \text{Max Capacity} = 15.0\text{ g/dL} \times 1.34\text{ mL O}_2/\text{g} = 20.10\text{ mL O}_2/\text{dL}

derivation_steps.explanation: Compute net O2 unloaded per dL of blood (and per 50 dL = 5.0 L Cardiac Output):
derivation_steps.equation_latex: \Delta [\text{O}_2]_{\text{unloaded}} = 20.10\text{ mL/dL} \times (0.9757 - 0.7544) = 20.10 \times 0.2213 = 4.45\text{ mL O}_2/\text{dL} \quad (222.5\text{ mL O}_2/\text{min at CO}=5\text{ L/min})

solved_problems.final_answer: (a) Arterial saturation = 97.6%, Venous saturation = 75.4%; (b) 4.45 mL O2 unloaded per dL of blood (~223 mL O2/min delivered to tissues at rest).

Solve α = 1 + [I] / K_i = 3.25 for K_i (with [I] = 4.0 μM):

(b) Diagnose the primary acid-base disturbance and the physiological compensatory mechanism.

practice_problems.question: If atherosclerotic plaque narrows the internal radius (r) of a coronary artery to 50% (1/2) of its original radius while vessel length and blood viscosity remain constant, by what factor does hemodynamic resistance (R) across that segment increase, and how does blood flow (Q) change at constant pressure?
practice_problems.bold_answer: Resistance increases 16-fold (2^4); Blood flow drops to 1/16 (6.25%) of normal
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: By Poiseuille's Law (R = 8ηL / πr^4), resistance is inversely proportional to the 4th power of radius. Halving the radius (r_2 = 0.5 r_1) increases resistance by (1 / 0.5)^4 = 2^4 = 16-fold, reducing flow Q = ΔP / R to 1/16 (6.25%) of its original value.

practice_problems.question: An enzyme follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics with K_m = 4.0 mM. At what substrate concentration [S] will the initial reaction velocity (V_0) reach 80% of V_max (V_0 = 0.80 V_max)?
Why is acute severe Hyperkalemia (elevation of extracellular plasma [K+]_out from 4.0 mM to 9.0 mM, e.g., in renal failure or massive crush injury) a life-threatening cardiac emergency?
practice_problems.bold_answer: Elevating [K+]_out makes E_K less negative (from -95 mV to -73 mV), chronically depolarizing the resting myocardium and inactivating voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav1.5) into diastolic cardiac arrest
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: By the Nernst equation, E_K = 61.5 log10(9.0 / 140) = -73.3 mV (compared to -95.0 mV at 4.0 mM). Sustained resting depolarization locks the fast inactivation h-gates of cardiac voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav1.5) in the closed state, abolishing Phase 0 conduction and causing fatal arrhythmias / cardiac arrest.

case_study.title: Clinical Pathophysiology Case Study: Cholera Toxin Gαs/CFTR Secretory Diarrhea & Oral Rehydration Therapy (SGLT1 Symport Rescue)
case_study.scenario: A patient in Kolkata presents with profuse 'rice-water' secretory diarrhea (losing >1 L of isotonic fluid per hour), severe dehydration, hypotension, and hypokalemic metabolic acidosis following ingestion of water contaminated with Vibrio cholerae. Intravenous saline stabilizes blood pressure, while drinking plain water fails to halt fluid loss—yet drinking WHO Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS, containing equimolar Glucose + NaCl) rapidly restores intestinal water absorption.
case_study.mechanistic_analysis: Vibrio cholerae secretes Cholera Toxin (AB5 enterotoxin). The B-pentamer binds GM1 gangliosides on intestinal crypt enterocytes, delivering the catalytic A1 subunit into the cytosol. CTA1 covalently transfers an ADP-ribose group from NAD+ onto Arg201 of the Gαs subunit, abolishing its intrinsic GTPase activity and locking Gαs-GTP permanently ON. Intracellular cAMP surges 100-fold, hyperactivating PKA, which phosphorylates and opens apical CFTR Cl- channels while inhibiting NHE3 Na+/H+ exchangers. Massive Cl- and Na+ efflux drags water osmotically into the intestinal lumen. Drinking plain water cannot be absorbed because cAMP blocks standard Na+ absorption; however, the apical SGLT1 (2 Na+ : 1 Glucose secondary active symporter) on villus enterocytes is completely unaffected by cAMP! Providing equimolar glucose + Na+ in WHO-ORS drives coupled Na+ and glucose uptake across the brush border, creating an osmotic gradient that pulls water back into the bloodstream.

quiz.question: During an action potential in a myelinated human axon, what prevents the action potential from propagating backward toward the cell body (soma)?
options: Myelin sheaths contain one-way mechanical valves at the Nodes of Ranvier

The trailing membrane segment just behind the advancing spike is in its Absolute Refractory Period because voltage-gated Na+ channel inactivation gates (h-gates) remain closed until the membrane repolarizes
The Na+/K+-ATPase pump reverses direction during the overshoot phase
GABAergic interneurons hyperpolarize the trailing node at every millisecond
quiz.explanation: Immediately following depolarization at a Node of Ranvier, local voltage-gated Na+ channels enter the inactivated state (ball-and-chain h-gate plugged). Until the membrane repolarizes toward resting potential, those channels cannot reopen, making the upstream segment refractory and forcing orthodromic (forward) propagation.

quiz.question: How does 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) facilitate oxygen transfer from maternal adult blood (HbA, α2β2) to fetal blood (HbF, α2γ2) across the placenta?
options: 2,3-BPG binds tightly to fetal HbF to increase its oxygen affinity above that of Myoglobin

Fetal γ-globin chains substitute neutral Ser143 for positively charged His143, reducing 2,3-BPG binding so HbF remains in the higher-affinity R-state (P50 ≈ 19 mmHg) relative to maternal HbA (P50 ≈ 27 mmHg)
2,3-BPG oxidizes maternal Fe2+ to Fe3+ methemoglobin in the placental intervillous space
2,3-BPG acts as a competitive inhibitor at the heme iron binding site of HbA
quiz.explanation: 2,3-BPG is a highly anionic metabolite that binds the positively charged central cavity of T-state deoxy-HbA, lowering its O2 affinity. Because fetal γ-subunits lack His143, 2,3-BPG binds weakly to HbF, keeping the HbF dissociation curve left-shifted (higher affinity) so O2 flows down an affinity gradient from maternal HbA to fetal HbF.

quiz.question: In the renal nephron, why is the Thick Ascending Limb (TAL) of the Loop of Henle referred to as the 'diluting segment' of the kidney?
options: It secretes pure water into the tubular lumen via Aquaporin-2 channels

Its apical NKCC2 cotransporters actively reabsorb Na+, K+, and Cl- into the medullary interstitium while the epithelium is completely impermeable to water, leaving the luminal fluid hypo-osmotic (~100 mOsm/L)
It filters plasma proteins out of the vasa recta
It converts urea into ammonia to dilute the urine
quiz.explanation: The Thick Ascending Limb lacks aquaporin water channels and is impermeable to water, yet actively pumps Na+, K+, and 2Cl- out of the filtrate via NKCC2. This simultaneously builds the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium (for countercurrent multiplication) and dilutes the tubular fluid entering the distal convoluted tubule to ~100 mOsm/L.

research_corner.paper_title: A Quantitative Description of Membrane Current and Its Application to Conduction and Excitation in Nerve (Hodgkin & Huxley, 1952) & Stereochemistry of Cooperative Effects in Haemoglobin (Perutz, Nature 1970)

imrad_breakdown.abstract_summary: Hodgkin and Huxley (1952) used the voltage-clamp technique on the squid giant axon to separate ionic currents into Na+ and K+ conductances and formulate the differential equations governing the action potential. Max Perutz (1970) compared high-resolution X-ray crystal structures of oxy- and deoxy-hemoglobin to reveal the T-to-R quaternary salt-bridge switch underlying allosteric cooperativity and the Bohr effect.
imrad_breakdown.key_method: Axial wire space-clamped and voltage-clamped electrophysiology in Loligo giant axons with choline-substituted Na+-free seawater; X-ray crystallography of horse and human hemoglobin at 2.8 Å resolution.
imrad_breakdown.critical_takeaway: Complex organ-level physiological phenomena—from nerve impulse propagation to systemic oxygen transport—emerge directly from quantifiable conformational transitions in transmembrane channels and allosteric proteins.
